title: What are the tyre strategy options for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix?
excerpt:
In other years, four different manufacturers in the first four grid slots would have been cause for note, now it’s merely business-as-usual in an exceptionally competitive 2026 season. One thing that did raise eyebrows, however, is the margin of George Russell’s eventual pole position.

Mercedes have looked rapid all weekend, but with championship leader Kimi Antonelli clipping a wall in Q1, Russell’s run to fifth pole of the season was serene – but his eight-tenths of a second margin to second-placed Charles Leclerc was exceptional.

But what do we have in store on Saturday? Almost certainly a one-stop race, but myriad possibilities within that. All three tyre compounds are in contention, the pit windows are wide, and, while it’s never particularly easy to pass in Baku, the combination of active aero and greater energy deployment options suggest we’re going to see something a bit different…

title: What the teams said – Qualifying in Azerbaijan
excerpt:
Mercedes

George Russell looked quick again from the off on Friday, as the Mercedes driver went into Qualifying as one of the heavy favourites for pole. He delivered just that, grabbing his first pole since Austria in what was an incredibly dominant performance – gapping the field by over eight tenths of a second. But while there was jubilation on Russell’s side of the garage, there was shock on Kimi Antonelli’s. He clipped the walls and damaged his car badly enough to park up. That was in Q1, and while his first lap time was enough to make Q2, he took no further part and has to start down the order tomorrow.

Kimi Antonelli, 16th, No time set in Q2

"First of all, congratulations to George. He's done an great job all weekend and fully deserves pole position.

On my side, it's obviously frustrating because the car felt good from FP3 onwards and the pace was there. We had a stronger headwind into Turn One than on the previous lap and the grip level had changed quite a lot, so the car had more grip than I expected. It's a shame because I felt we had enough pace to get through comfortably and fight further up the order. I tried my best to bring the car back to the pits, but unfortunately the damage was too much. The team made the right call to stop the car and protect it.

The positive is that we've shown strong pace all weekend and the car has felt good. Starting further back will make things difficult at a track where overtaking isn't easy, but I've shown before that I can bounce back from setbacks and my focus is already on tomorrow. We'll do everything we can to move forward, score good points and maximise the result for the team."

George Russell, 1st, 1:42.526

"That lap was unbelievable. Given how tight things have been all weekend, I was shocked when I saw the gap. The lap felt incredibly good, but I certainly wasn't expecting that result.

The plan was always to stay on the same set of tyres. The first run was a banker because I knew there was more time to find, and I wanted to push the limits on the second lap. Everything came together. The car felt really hooked up and I was able to get the most out of it.

With Max, both Ferraris and Kimi all looking strong this weekend, it's going to be important to get a good start, maximise every opportunity and execute a clean race. I've felt good in every session and that qualifying lap was one of the most satisfying I've done. The focus now is on tomorrow and making sure we convert today's result into the best possible outcome."

Bradley Lord, Mercedes Deputy Team Principal

"That was an amazing lap from George! He topped every segment of qualifying, honed his approach with each lap, and then delivered a dominant lap when it mattered most. We approached qualifying like a wet session, aiming to be on track throughout and not at the mercy of yellow flags, and that included being first car on track in Q3 - and the first car to complete the session. George executed everything cleanly and thoroughly deserved pole.

Tomorrow won't be straightforward. Around Baku, the tow and energy deployment characteristics of these cars make it difficult to control the race from the front, so there will be plenty to manage across the distance. But his target is absolutely clear.

It was a frustrating session for Kimi, particularly given the pace he and the car have shown all weekend. He clipped the wall in Turn One after the car gripped up more than he expected as he committed to the corner, and Race Control instructed him to park the car shortly after. Incidents like this are part and parcel of a long season and can happen around a street circuit like this where the margins are small; it's another moment of learning.

Kimi has shown several times this season that he is able to put setbacks behind him quickly. The pace has been there throughout the weekend, and the objective tomorrow will be to recover as many positions as possible. The team will repair and prepare the car, and we're confident he can fight his way forward in the race."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"Congratulations to George and the team on a well deserved pole. He has been strong all weekend and looked to take another step into qualifying. By the final session it didn't look like there was anyone to challenge him and his final lap was exceptional.

Kimi had a tough time with a mistake that took him out of the running from early in Q1 when he misjudged the entry to Turn 1. He's clearly disappointed, especially having seen the potential that was in the car today, but we'll look at plans that allow him to mount a strong recovery.

With George we need to see if we've got the pace to control the race, but even if that is strong, it can be a difficult race to manage given the risk of incidents coupled with the fact that we may be having to cover off numerous threats from behind.

The car has been competitive from the first session and that's given us a great opportunity tomorrow. Converting that into a strong result won't be straightforward around Baku, but we've put ourselves in a good position and now need to execute cleanly across the whole race."

title: What To Watch For in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix
excerpt:
From George Russell with a huge chance to secure his first win in seven rounds to Kimi Antonelli fighting through the field, and from strong performances from current and former Red Bull drivers to the potential for a race-changing moment, here are five things to keep an eye on as we celebrate a decade of racing around the Baku City Circuit.

1. Russell’s golden opportunity for a third win

Given the performance potential of the Mercedes this year, it still feels surprising that George Russell has won just two races so far in 2026.

Russell is second in the Drivers’ Championship but endured a tough run during the middle of the season before an uptick in form since returning from the summer shutdown.

title: ‘I don’t deserve all the s*** I have on my back’ – Ocon
excerpt:
It was a classic case of mixed emotions for Haas drivers Esteban Ocon and Ollie Bearman after a tight Qualifying session in Baku.

Both men were fighting for a place in Q3, a sign of much improved form, and both were left disappointed as they missed out.

However, while Bearman saw a glass half full and called the upswing in form “invigorating”, his team mate was left fuming after his final Q2 run was spoiled by a yellow flag.

Ocon’s frustration was perhaps not surprising given that at times this season Haas have been fighting to get out of Q1, and on a weekend when the package was clearly stronger than it’s been for a while, the pieces didn’t fall into place.

Throw in his clear hint on Wednesday as a “free agent” that he could be out of a job for next year and it’s understandable that he saw a missed opportunity.

Having been P12 in Friday’s FP3 session, Ocon was an encouraging P10 in Q1 which indicated that progression to Q3 was on the cards. However, he didn’t get a clean lap at the end of Q2, and found himself stuck in P14.

“Unbelievable,” he said. “We were on for a Q3 lap, the car was working well. We don't have many chances like this when the car is working well. It hasn’t been working throughout the whole season. We improved things, but we had a Q3 car today.

“And the yellow flag, basically. I got a gust of wind the lap before, but I was on for a Q3 lap as well, and then I did the same lap time again, arriving to Turn 15. I don’t know who went off, but I had to back off on the exit to make sure that I was not going to get any penalty.

“And yeah, I did exactly the same lap time, so I lost what, three, four tenths, with that? Unbelievable. I just have no words.”

It’s not been an easy season for the Frenchman, who has often struggled with the VF-26, and been hampered at times by inconsistencies in aero parts.

“It’s a different race weekend, same s***,” he said. “It’s always something going on on my side, if it’s either the car, if it's something else, now yellow flag, Safety Cars, whatever.

“But I don’t deserve all the s*** I have on my back at the moment. So, I don’t know. I might need to take a good shower...”

Asked if, as a top 10 contender, the car was the best he’d had all year, he said: “I mean, yes, but I think we’re very far from where it should be.

“We need to fight in the top 10 tomorrow now, because we are 14th, so we’re not in the top 10. At the end of the day, yes, we were competitive, but we can’t get there. Never – it’s never happening.”

It was also a frustrating Q2 session for Bearman. He was in the top 10 when he completed his final run earlier than most, but was then bumped out by others who ran later. He ended up in P11.

“We did it quite early,” he said. “I caught the yellow flag on my final lap, and I was doing the same lap time, but I also had a better track position, I had a better slipstream, so maybe I would have had a bit more lap time in it.

“But for me, the tyres were their best a bit earlier in the session on Lap 2, when I did my lap.

“So, it’s one of those things. What can we do? It hurts because, of course, it’s been a really good weekend considering that I didn’t run yesterday in FP2, and all of those things mean that actually I think we’re doing very well considering everything.

“It always hurts – but today a little bit more. But the only consolation is that I think tomorrow there can be some good opportunities on a track like this.”

Despite his disappointment, Bearman saw the positives in the pace of the car. “I think it’s an invigorating feeling,” he said. “And as much as it really sucks to be knocked out, the fact that we’re even considering to be in Q3 means that we’re doing something right.

“And the car has been strong since Monza, since we brought the update. It’s incredibly strong in low-speed as well. It’s just a shame that we lose so much on the straights.”

title: Piastri assesses 'surprise' Qualifying result in Baku
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri says starting from P3 in Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix is a "big surprise" after both McLaren cars had appeared to lack pace during practice.

Early in Q3, however, Piastri and team mate Lando Norris put in times that saw them provisionally lock out the front row, with the Australian's best time of 1m 43.364s ultimately just one thousandth of a second off Charles Leclerc in P2.

Before Qualifying, the McLaren pair were not really being mentioned in the hunt for pole, having only placed as high as sixth in practice.

But come Friday afternoon in Baku, something seemed to click. While they couldn't hold on to the front row – Norris had a lock up on his final run which saw him finish fifth fastest – Piastri only missed out by the narrowest of margins.

“It’s not the first time that’s happened to us this year,” explained Piastri. “We seem like we’re a bit on the back foot through practice, we come out in Qualifying and, yeah, we just find that bit extra.

“I was pretty surprised to see us 1-2 after the first lap of Q3, but unfortunately, we had no hope against George [Russell]. So, happy with how the weekend’s gone so far.”

From P3, Piastri will surely start the Grand Prix with the hope of a podium finish, but has mixed fortunes at the circuit. In 2024 he won after defending from Leclerc for more than 30 laps but, a year later, he crashed in Qualifying and in the race – significantly denting his title hopes.

The 25-year-old is staying cautiously optimistic about his chances this time out though. “Difficult to know,” he said when asked about his chances. “I think, honestly, our race pace [on Thursday] almost looked better than our one-lap pace. So from that side of things I was pretty happy, but we’ll have to wait and see.

“Obviously, it’s always a bit of chaos around here, so we’ll see what we get.”

Meanwhile, Norris cut a disappointed figure with his fifth-fastest time – compounded by the lock up on his final attempt – saying afterwards: “I was already up I think a little bit on the first two corners. I mean, when we’re so far off, I’m going to try and push to get a… I don’t think P1 was possible today, because George did an amazing job, but I’d rather try and push for P1 and P2 but make a mistake than settle for a P5, or a P3, or a P4.

“It’s the way it is sometimes. Obviously we’re a long way off, but still there or thereabouts.”

“I’ve been driving very well this weekend,” added the reigning World Champion. “It’s just some problems that we have with the car that just limits my lap time a little bit. Hopefully we can fix them.

“We’re probably not going to fix them tomorrow, which means we’re in for a tough race. We’ve got some things we need to fix on the car, because I’m just at a deficit to the other car at the minute.”

title: Perez given penalty after Azerbaijan Qualifying infringement
excerpt:
Sergio Perez has been handed a penalty for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix after the Cadillac driver was found to have impeded Oscar Piastri in Qualifying.

The Mexican, who has won on the streets of Baku twice before, had high hopes on Friday of achieving Cadillac's best Qualifying result of the season after encouraging pace in practice, but Perez ultimately failed to advance into Q2 and finished P20.

But post-Qualifying, stewards investigated an on-track incident where Perez had blocked Piastri while the McLaren driver was on a flying lap.

The incident took place throgh Turns 18, 19 and 20 while Perez was on a preparation lap and weaving to warm his tyres.

The stewards noted that he "had received two warnings of Piastri approaching and did not manage his preparation lap in accordance with the specific traffic-management instructions".

As a consequence, "Piastri confirmed that he had to lift because of Perez, although he did not consider that he ultimately lost significant lap time as a consequence".

The stewards "considered whether the incident was dangerous but, having reviewed the evidence and heard both drivers, determined that it was not", but added that "the fact that Piastri was required to lift was sufficient to establish that he had been unnecessarily impeded".

As a result, Perez has been handed a three-place grid penalty for Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Perez will still maintain his position of P20 though, as the Aston Martins of Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll are set to serve larger grid penalties for engine changes.

Further up the order the Williams of Carlos Sainz, who had qualified in ninth, was hit with a five-place grid penalty for a failure to slow for yellow flags.

title: Sainz hit with five-place grid penalty for Azerbaijan GP
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has been given a five-place grid penalty for Saturday’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix after the stewards found him guilty of failing to slow for yellow flags in Qualifying.

Sainz had taken his heavily upgraded Williams to the final Q3 phase and ninth on the grid at the Baku City Circuit, only to be noted for a potential rule breach.

After hearing from Sainz and a Williams team representative, and reviewing the range of data available to them, the stewards ultimately deemed that the Spaniard had broken the rules.

Sainz was subsequently given a five-place grid drop, meaning he falls from P9 to P14 – promoting Franco Colapinto, Ollie Bearman, Liam Lawson, team mate Alex Albon and Esteban Ocon.

“Single yellow flags were displayed in Marshalling Sectors 4 and 5, in particular after Turn 2 and on the approach to Turn 3,” read the stewards’ decision document, with Lando Norris going off track ahead of Sainz during Q3. “The yellow indications were clearly visible and SAI had also received a radio warning from the team: ‘Yellow ahead, lift’. SAI confirmed at the hearing that he was aware of the yellow flag situation.

“SAI explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the yellow area as a whole. He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a ‘global lift’ covering the consecutive yellow sectors.

“He further explained that the car which had originally caused the yellow was no longer in the run-off area and that he expected the yellow flags to be withdrawn.

“The stewards did not accept this interpretation. Where consecutive marshalling sectors are subject to yellow flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant reaction to reduce speed in each individual yellow marshalling sector. A reduction in a subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the preceding yellow sector.

“The obligation is also not dependent on the driver’s own assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of the yellow sector.

“The telemetry clearly showed that SAI’s reaction to the yellow occurred only in Marshalling Sector 5. There was no meaningful reduction in speed in Marshalling Sector 4, which could realistically be attributed to a response to the yellow. Indeed, SAI recorded his fastest time of the session in Marshalling Sector 4.

“The stewards therefore did not accept that the subsequent lift in Marshalling Sector 5 constituted a sufficient ‘global’ response covering both sectors. This is distinguishable from cases where the telemetry demonstrates a significant response to the yellow even though the overall sector time reduction is relatively small.

“In the present case, SAI was aware of the yellow, had received an explicit warning from the team, the yellow indications were clearly visible and the telemetry established that he did not demonstrate the required reaction in Marshalling Sector 4.

“The stewards therefore determine that SAI failed to sufficiently reduce speed under the single yellow flag in Marshalling Sector 4. The standard penalty under the Penalty Guidelines for this infringement during Qualifying is a drop of five grid positions.”

Sainz was also handed two penalty points, giving him a total of four for the 12-month period – as set out in F1’s penalty regulations.

title: Gasly buoyed by Alpine gains after Baku double Q3 appearance
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly revealed that he could’ve extracted “even more” from Alpine’s performance in Qualifying without the disruption of yellow flags, concluding that he has “good confidence” in their potential at the Baku City Circuit.

A few weeks on from the Frenchman’s magnificent maiden pole in Italy, Alpine once again look like they can contend for valuable points, with Gasly peaking as high as P6 in Qualifying before settling for P7.

They are embroiled in an ongoing fight to be named ‘best of the rest’ against Racing Bulls, so with both Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad set to start outside of the top 10 for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, this weekend represents a fantastic chance for Alpine to close the nine-point gap.

Reflecting on the session, Gasly said: “Very good work this weekend in terms of car set-up and getting to a place where I can really be comfortable with the balance and commit everywhere. I’m very pleased.

“Strong Qualifying – honestly, our last two runs were both compromised with people going off, so I think there was even more in it. I think [getting] ahead of Lewis [Hamilton] was possible.

“We don’t control it, we were just unlucky that people kept going off in front of us. Overall, bigger picture, I’m just happy with the car we have. It’s a good baseline that also gives me good confidence for tomorrow and the coming races.

“[Ferrari] probably have more pace, but I think it’s probably the time I’ve felt best in Baku in terms of car balance. It’s always tricky with tyres etc., but at least I was really able to throw the car around and play with it. We’re starting in a good place for some good points.”

The team were able to celebrate both cars progressing to Q3 as Franco Colapinto also squeezed through, but he failed to set a representative lap time in the final segment after locking up at Turn 15.

Settling for P10, the Argentine was understandably not as satisfied as his team mate despite contributing to Alpine’s third double Q3 appearance of the 2026 season.

“I think generally there’s still a lot to improve,” Colapinto explained. “It’s not been an easy session. I lacked a bit of pace, but then Q3 was not very well executed – I had this big lock-up and then I had really big vibrations for the last lap.

“We’re still doing the steps, we’re improving. I just lacked a bit in that Q3 to have a better result, but I will try to fight tomorrow and go forward. It’s good to have both cars in Q3.

“I’m not very comfortable in the hard braking zones, and here it’s full of those. It doesn’t feel so easy at the minute but we’ll try to work for tomorrow.”

title: Max Verstappen confirms upcoming F1 grid penalty
excerpt:
Max Verstappen is expecting a grid drop at some point in the near future.

Max Verstappen has confirmed that he is due to take a grid penalty at some point during the 2026 F1 season.

The Dutchman's comments came after he endured a difficult qualifying session in Baku, where he finished eighth in the order.

Verstappen was heard complaining about the behaviour of the car over the team radio and explained after the session that he had an issue with his engine.

Red Bull is due to carry out a change of the components it labelled “faulty” ahead of Sunday's race, which will not incur a grid drop if they are from the pool of elements that have already been used this year.

However, Verstappen is not expecting to go the rest of the year without having to go outside of the penalty-free allocation.

“A penalty is bound to come at some point,” Verstappen told select media including RacingNews365. “That was always clear.”

When asked why it wasn't done for Baku, Verstappen stated: “The problem on the straight is that everyone goes from a full battery to completely empty.

“You can’t use the battery. Going from 100 to zero is the same for everyone.”

Driver

Verstappen expands on engine frustrations

Verstappen's P8 result is among the worst that he has suffered this year.

While he had issues with his car on Friday, his result was also hindered by a yellow flag, which forced him to abort his final effort.

However, his primary frustrations related to the car itself, as he explained: “You’re so slow on the straights.

“Because of that, you use up more battery power coming out of the turns to try to compensate.

“On other sections, you go into the superclip, very aggressively. Everything was out of whack, it just wasn’t working anymore.

“You spend more time on the straight because you’re going slower, and that naturally causes you to use more power.

“It’s the same with Honda, they clip more than anyone else, too. You spend more time at full throttle."

title: Oscar Piastri offers cunning George Russell idea in expected Baku brawl
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has quipped that he will attach a "tow bar" to the back of George Russell's dominant Mercedes in an expected tough Azerbaijan GP fight.

Piastri secured third on the grid in Baku, but was 0.838s down on Mercedes' Russell who recorded the largest pole margin in over three years, as he crushed the field to secure P1 after team-mate Kimi Antonelli hit a wall in Q1 and will start 16th.

Piastri, who was just 0.001s slower than Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in the fight for a front-row berth, is in a McLaren MCL40 machine which has struggled with straight-line speed all season, with the 2.2km-long Baku straight exposing this weakness in the package.

Elsewhere around the lap, the McLaren is more competitive, meaning Piastri is engaged in the fight with the Ferraris, Red Bulls and sister McLaren of Lando Norris, who goes from fifth, in the fight behind Russell.

So dominant has the W17 been, Piastri came up with a cunning idea to ensure he can keep Russell honest during the grand prix.

"If he’s got a tow bar that I can hook onto the back of, maybe," Piastri quipped when asked by media, including RacingNews365, if he could challenge Russell.

"We’ll see what we can do. I think the Mercedes look incredibly quick here, but I think everyone else looks like they’re in a similar-ish kind of pack.

"Our race pace looked pretty good [in practice], to be honest. So, yeah, I think we can hang on and battle in the pack behind George, and we'll see what lap Kimi starts coming through as well."

The article continues below.

Piastri primed in P3 for Azerbaijan GP

Turning to his own performance, Piastri spoke of how the car "came alive" during a tricky session to extract potential.

"I think some laps here and there have been strong, but it’s been a lot in between that haven’t been very strong, and I feel like we’ve been reasonable at points, but our car needs some specific things, and trying to find those things on a street circuit is really tough," he said.

"In qualifying we just come alive a little bit more, everything becomes a little bit easier, and it’s a bit easier for us to get the pace out of the car. But, no, on a personal level I feel like we’ve been building up well and, yeah, was pretty happy with my lap in Q3."

title: Liam Lawson pins Baku struggles on 'frustrating' area: 'We’re a lot worse now'
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has pointed to Racing Bulls' straight-line struggles as a "frustrating" shortcoming during qualifying in Baku.

The Faenza-based squad has often been the benchmark team in the midfield this year with impressive form in both qualifying and race trim.

However, it was unable to get itself involved in the fight for the top 10 on Friday during qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, with both Lawson and team-mate Arvid Lindblad failing to get inside the top 10.

While Lawson was content with the execution of his lap, he stated he was let down by the car's straight-line speed.

"The lap was very good up until the last couple of corners, and I just struggled with overheating," Lawson told media including RacingNews365.

"I didn't get a tow as well, which is really powerful here.

"Especially for us this weekend, we've been pretty slow down the straights. It's frustrating.

"I actually think we've done quite a good job with the car and looking back to some tracks earlier in the year, or tracks where we've been quite competitive, I actually feel like we've made a step with the car.

"We're just a lot worse now down the straights compared to some of the other teams with other power units, especially on these tracks with long straights.

"It's pretty frustrating."

[Article continues below]

Lawson sets sights on Baku points

Lawson ended the session in 12th place, but has already been bumped up one spot on the grid due to a penalty for Carlos Sainz.

This weekend is the first for Lawson since his return to Racing Bulls, having stood in for Isack Hadjar at the previous three rounds.

As he takes up a starting position on the fringes of the top 10, the New Zealander has set his sights on adding to his points tally.

"I'd love to score points," he said.

"That's the target [for the race], but we have got work to do."

title: The 10 biggest F1 pole margins across the last decade after George Russell demolition
excerpt:
Check out the top 10 biggest pole margins across the last decade in F1 following George Russell's stunning Azerbaijan GP qualifying performance.

George Russell produced one of the most dominant qualifying laps of the season in Baku, putting his Mercedes on pole for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix by 0.837 seconds over Charles Leclerc's Ferrari.

It was a scarcely believable gap around a street circuit where tenths, not tenths of a second gaps like this, usually separate the front two.

The margin instantly raises a question: where does it sit among the biggest pole advantages of the past decade?

The answer places Russell in rare company, behind only three drivers who have ever qualified by a bigger buffer in the last ten years.

Check out the biggest grand prix pole margins of the last decade below!

Driver

George Russell

British

63

1. Max Verstappen, 2023 Canadian Grand Prix, 1.244s

Max Verstappen's 2023 Canadian Grand Prix pole remains the benchmark, the Dutchman beating the field by 1.244 seconds in changeable conditions that turned qualifying into a lottery he alone seemed to solve with total command of the tricky Montreal grip levels.

2. Lewis Hamilton, 2020 Styrian Grand Prix, 1.216s

Lewis Hamilton's 2020 Styrian Grand Prix effort follows at 1.216 seconds, a lap delivered at the Red Bull Ring during Formula 1's pandemic-disrupted restart, where Mercedes' pace advantage over the field was at its most brutal.

3. Lewis Hamilton, 2017 Italian Grand Prix, 1.148s

Hamilton also holds third spot, his 2017 Italian Grand Prix pole at Monza coming in 1.148 seconds clear, a staggering figure at a circuit where slipstreaming usually compresses the times.

4. George Russell, 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix, 0.837s

Russell's Baku lap slots in fourth at 0.837 seconds, ahead of two Verstappen poles from 2023 and 2022. It represents the biggest pole margin since the introduction of the new power unit regulations.

5. Max Verstappen, 2022 Belgian Grand Prix, 0.820s

Verstappen's Spa pole that year yielded a 0.820-second margin, underlining the Red Bull's straight-line advantage around the Ardennes circuit.

6. Max Verstappen, 2022 Emilia Romagna Grand Prix, 0.779s

His Emilia Romagna Grand Prix pole in Imola came in at 0.779 seconds amid difficult, drying conditions that made setting a clean lap a considerable challenge.

7. Nico Rosberg, 2016 European Grand Prix, 0.757s

Nico Rosberg's 2016 European Grand Prix pole in Baku itself, back when the circuit ran under that title, produced a 0.757-second gap during Mercedes' near-total qualifying supremacy that campaign.

8. Charles Leclerc, 2019 Belgian Grand Prix, 0.748s

Charles Leclerc's 2019 Belgian Grand Prix pole for Ferrari came in at 0.748 seconds, part of the run of form that preceded his maiden win at Spa that weekend.

9. Lewis Hamilton, 2018 Belgian Grand Prix, 0.726s

Hamilton's 2018 Belgian Grand Prix pole rounds out another Spa entry at 0.726 seconds, a lap that underlined Mercedes' one-lap edge over Ferrari that year.

10. Nico Rosberg, 2016 Russian Grand Prix, 0.706s

Rosberg completes the list with his 2016 Russian Grand Prix pole in Sochi, a 0.706-second margin that came during the German's imperious run to that year's title.

title: Isack Hadjar highlights agonising Baku consequence of Red Bull absence
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar marked his F1 return in strong fashion by securing a second-row starting spot on Sunday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix grid.

Isack Hadjar has suggested he would have claimed a front-row spot on the Azerbaijan Grand Prix starting grid had he not missed the last three events.

Following an injury picked up during the summer break, Hadjar was ruled out of the following three rounds in Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid.

He was deemed fit enough to return in Baku and fired himself into P4 for his second-best qualifying result of the campaign.

Hadjar insisted he took a measured approach to his return, having not driven the car since the end of July.

“I'm happy about the approach,” Hadjar told media including RacingNews365.

“I just took it very slowly yesterday until Q1, when I made a step, but I just felt like I needed more laps in the car to actually be second on the grid.

“It's quite close ahead. I'm happy with myself, just if I had been racing the last three races, I would definitely be second on the grid.

“I just feel like it's a tough track to come back to after two months.”

[Article continues below]

Driver

Isack Hadjar

French

6

Hadjar drove 'under the limit' to avoid car damage

With Baku being a high-speed circuit with very little margin for error, practice and qualifying saw several yellow flags deployed as drivers ran wide.

Hadjar, however, insisted that he purposely drove away from the limit right until crunch time in qualifying in order to keep himself out of trouble.

“I told myself it's mandatory not to touch the wall or anything, for a comeback, there's no point taking a lot of risks,” he said.

“I was really driving a bit under the limit the whole weekend in the very tight sections.

“I just did that natural step in Q3, but I had it really under control, and I started having a bit more fun.

“At the end of Q2, I was actually taking risks, and I went away for the first time this weekend, I had the lock-up.”

title: Lando Norris demands McLaren investigation into 'very painful' car issue
excerpt:
Lando Norris wants McLaren to urgently look at its straight-line speed deficit after a huge gap to Mercedes in Azerbaijan GP qualifying.

Norris qualified in fifth place in Baku, but was 1.146s slower than pole-sitter George Russell in Q3 as the MCL40's weakness in a staight line was exposed.

McLaren's chassis, despite its recent upgrades, is still a draggy car, meaning on circuits with uber-long straights, such as the 2.2km long one in Baku's Sector 3, the car of Norris and Piastri is struggling.

Some of the deficit to Russell can be explained by the fact Norris did not complete his final flying lap in Q3 after locking up and running wide at Turn 3, but the reigning F1 champion was not overly pleased with the situation as he voiced his demands for McLaren to look into the issue - something he felt was exacerbated on his car compared to team-mate Piastri, who took third and was 0.308s faster.

"I don't think we found any pace; why would you say that?" Norris shot back to media, including RacingNews365, during the post-session media pen.

"Relative to others, we did, but I always expect that with lower fuel, I am still eight-tenths off pole, and to be honest, most of our time loss to them is still in the straights, and there is not a lot I can do about that.

"I've been comfortable in the car all weekend, and on the last lap, I made a mistake and paid the price, but I am at a point in the championship where I have to go for pole or I kind of die trying, and I paid the price for pushing too much.

"It is an area we just need to look at because we just look a step worse than Mercedes in everything straight-line related, so it is tough, especially with my car, which is worse than [Piastri's].

"So it is making our life very painful.

"There are multiple issues, and there are more on my car for some reason than the other car, so we have to understand why.

"We need to take a big step in that direction if you want to be competitive on any straight-line speed track for the rest of the season."

Norris seeking McLaren investigation

Further explaining the issue of a lack of straight-line speed compared to Piastri, Norris kept details close, but said he was having to push "more."

"I'm basically having to push more than Oscar to try and make up for the [lack of] straight-line speed, and Mercedes have a very efficient car; they have done for years," he said.

title: Carlos Sainz delivered crushing Azerbaijan GP grid drop after breakthrough result
excerpt:
“Single Yellow Flags were displayed in Marshalling Sectors 4 and 5, in particular after Turn 2 and on the approach to Turn 3. The Yellow indications were clearly visible and SAI had also received a radio warning from the Team: “Yellow ahead, lift.” SAI confirmed at the hearing that he was aware of the Yellow Flag situation.

“SAI explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the Yellow area as a whole. He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a “global lift” covering the consecutive Yellow sectors.

“He further explained that the car which had originally caused the Yellow was no longer in the run-off area and that he expected the Yellow Flags to be withdrawn. The Stewards did not accept this interpretation.

“Where consecutive marshalling sectors are subject to Yellow Flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant reaction to reduce speed in each individual Yellow marshalling sector.

“A reduction in a subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the preceding Yellow sector. The obligation is also not dependent on the driver’s own assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of the Yellow sector.

“The telemetry clearly showed that SAI’s reaction to the Yellow occurred only in Marshalling Sector 5. There was no meaningful reduction in speed in Marshalling Sector 4 which could realistically be attributed to a response to the Yellow. Indeed, SAI recorded his fastest time of the session in Marshalling Sector 4.

“The Stewards therefore did not accept that the subsequent lift in Marshalling Sector 5 constituted a sufficient “global” response covering both sectors. This is distinguishable from cases where the telemetry demonstrates a significant response to the Yellow even though the overall sector time reduction is relatively small.

“In the present case, SAI was aware of the Yellow, had received an explicit warning from the Team, the Yellow indications were clearly visible and the telemetry established that he did not demonstrate the required reaction in Marshalling Sector 4.

“The Stewards therefore determine that SAI failed to sufficiently reduce speed under the Single Yellow Flag in Marshalling Sector 4.”

title: Sergio Perez handed Azerbaijan grid penalty after stewards investigation
excerpt:
Sergio Perez has been handed a three-place grid penalty by Azerbaijan Grand Prix stewards following an incident involving Oscar Piastri in qualifying.

During Q1 in Baku, Piastri was forced lift off during a flying lap through Turns 18,19, and 20 at the end of the lap to avoid the slow Cadillac of Perez.

Piastri was travelling around 300kph with Perez at 248kph as he continued a preparation lap, and, the stewards had found, was told twice of the McLaren approaching.

The race director's instructions inform drivers to stay on the right-hand side of the track during preparation laps, but Perez failed to do this as he was weaving to warm his tyres - thus causing Piastri to be impeded.

Piastri did tell the stewards that, although he lifted, he did not feel any significant time loss.

The stewards determined that the incident was not dangerous, but given Perez had received two warnings of Piastri's arrival, did not follow the instructions, and that Piastri was forced to lift, he was impeded.

As such, Perez received a three-place grid drop, which dropped him from P19 on the road to P20 on the grid as both Aston Martin drivers have received back-of-the-grid engine penalties, with Valtteri Bottas swapping places with his team-mate.

title: Lewis Hamilton bemoans key Baku burden: 'Such a pain in the ass'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton turned on an old nemesis to underline what has so far been a difficult Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Hamilton will start from sixth on the grid at the Baku City Circuit after finishing a staggering 1.3s behind lightning polesitter George Russell, and half a second adrift of Ferrari team-mate, Charles Leclerc, who joins the Mercedes driver on the front row.

The seven-time F1 champion conceded after qualifying that he has "been struggling all weekend to get the tyres working".

In trying to get heat into the Pirelli rubber ahead of his only push lap in Q3, Hamilton, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, said: "I was weaving to try and save my life, and I still couldn't get these stupid tyres working", before letting out a chuckle.

More seriously, he added: "They're such a pain in the ass. We need to bring back some good tyres."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton queries Ferrari run plan

Hamilton felt he was additionally compromised by Ferrari's late change of plan to only go for the one hot lap in Q3.

"Q1 was pretty okay," he said. "I felt the car wasn't too bad. In Q2, I started struggling even more with the rear tyres.

"After Q2, they decided to change the run plan and just do one run, which...I hadn't foreseen the fact that I would come out with no one ahead of me and just towing Charles the whole time."

Despite Leclerc's performance in claiming a front-row start, Hamilton feels Ferrari can only claim to have the third-quickest car in Baku behind Mercedes and Red Bull.

Surprisingly, Isack Hadjar, on his return to Red Bull after missing the last three races with a wrist injury, out-qualified Verstappen and will start fourth, four places ahead of the four-time champion, who later indicated he had an engine problem.

Hamilton feels it will be hard for him to make progress.

"Charles did a really good job," said Hamilton. "Right at the end, I gave him a really good tow all the way to the start line.

"But it'll be hard to overtake any other cars who are more competitive."

title: Furious Max Verstappen 'completely done' after latest Red Bull problem
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was an expected contender for Baku pole, only for a major problem to take any chance of fighting at the front away.

Max Verstappen felt "completely done" with Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying after suffering from Red Bull's latest problem, taking away any chance of a strong result.

Verstappen could only manage eighth place in qualifying following an issue with his battery, and the Dutchman was fuming afterwards.

For a long time it looked like a strong result was on the cards for Verstappen in Baku. The Red Bull driver had been running close behind an unstoppable George Russell for much of the session, but it all fell apart in Q3.

Verstappen reported that his car was struggling to charge and appeared to be caught out by a yellow flag as well.

Eighth was as good as it got, leaving him well adrift of team-mate Isack Hadjar, and the 28-year-old did not hold back when explaining what went wrong.

"The engine just wasn't working the whole of qualifying," Verstappen told Viaplay.

"We'd made one change to the car and that didn't really pay off either. But yeah, the car wasn't working. Compared to my team-mate I was already half a second down on the straights.

"You want to push on for the middle sector and suddenly the battery wasn't full. It's not charging, it's not working. And then they tell me I need to push with half a battery. I thought: just piss off. I was completely done with it for a moment."

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Verstappen had entered qualifying as a real contender for pole position, as the Red Bull star went quickest in final practice.

While George Russell unlocked exceptional pace in the final part of qualifying, a front row start was on the cards for Verstappen if not for the problems he faced.

"You prepare so well all weekend," added Verstappen. "The car is working well. Then it all falls apart in qualifying and you can't do anything with it anymore.

"After that aborted lap because the battery was half full, the tyre pressure also cooled down too much. You can't push because it's not working, so you can't get enough temperature into the tyres."

"So in the last lap as well I just didn't have the right grip, plus the same problem with the engine not working.

"The engine braking was also strange, sometimes it felt like you were pulling the handbrake in certain corners. Something is seriously wrong."

Asked whether the issue could be fixed before the race, Verstappen was uncertain.

"I don't know. They need to look into whether it can be solved with this engine. It's a shame of course when you've been so strong all weekend. Then they basically throw it away."

title: Kimi Antonelli explains Baku accident that has opened F1 title door
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has explained the sequence of events which led to his accident in Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying, which has slightly opened the title door for George Russell.

During Q1 in Baku, Antonelli clipped the inside wall of Turn 1, and although his time was enough for him to advance through to Q2, he took no part in the segment and will start 16th.

Antonelli had tried to bring the broken Mercedes back into the pits for running repairs, but was instructed by race engineer Peter Bonnington to pull off, so severe was the damage to the front-left of the W17.

In contrast, team-mate Russell roared to a dominant pole position, 0.837s faster than Charles Leclerc in second to give the Briton a prime opportunity to eat into the 81-point deficit he has to the Italian, who must now fight through the field to rescue a points score during the 51-lap race.

Reflecting, Antonelli explained how an unexpected level of grip had led to the "misjudgment."

"[In practice], yes, I did miss a lot of laps, but in FP3, I felt good, and it was just a misjudgment to be fair with the grip changing so much," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365.

"It was unnecessary in Q1, and it is a very good reminder that things like this don't go my way, so I need to do a better job.

"I had a lot more headwind compared to the lap before, so the front was much stronger, and I turned roughly in at the same spot, but obviously the car turned more, and I clipped the wall.

"It was very frustrating [to be told to stop]. I tried my best to come in, but they told me the damage was too big, so I had to bail out, which is even more annoying because I thought they could obviously repair it, as the lap was still okay to get through.

"But unfortunately, it was not possible, so we will reset and move on

"It's been very interrupted; I missed three-quarters of FP1 and FP2, so then you just don't get into the rhythm, but obviously, I made a mistake, so it is also on my side, but I definitely wasn't 100% there.

Antonelli mad

Speaking further on the incident, Antonelli called the error "very unnecessary" and said he was "very mad" about his first big error since crashing in FP3 in Australia, the season-opener.

"The grip was coming up very quickly, lap-by-lap," Antonelli explained to Sky Sports F1.

"So I turned in and sadly had a lot more front end compared to the lap before, and touched the wall.

"It is is a mistake from my side, it is very unnecessary.

"To be fair, I am very mad about it and will try to do better [in the race].

"The car has been very strong this weekend, and George has been doing incredibly well, so we will try our best [on Saturday], to recover as many places as is possible."
